name: The Canon of Medicine
info: The Canon of Medicine is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books compiled by Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and completed in 1025, which gathered the medical knowledge of the Islamic world and became a standard university textbook in Europe.

facts.made: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), who began it in Gorganj, continued it in Rey and completed it in Hamadan in 1025, drawing on Greco-Roman, Persian, Chinese and Indian medicine
facts.form: An Arabic encyclopedia of medicine in five books: principles and anatomy, a materia medica of about 800 simple substances, diseases by body part, diseases of more than one part, and a formulary of 650 compound drugs
facts.where: Read in Arabic and in Latin, Hebrew, Turkish and Persian translations; the earliest known copy of volume 5, dated 1052, is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto
facts.known: the five-book plan; the materia medica; seven rules for testing new drugs; descriptions of stroke and of the nervous system; the long treatment of fevers; its place as the standard medical textbook of European universities

t: Ibn Sina set out the medical knowledge of his time in five ordered books, fitting the traditions of Galen and Hippocrates into Aristotle's natural philosophy.
Its Latin translation entered European scholastic medicine, and university courses used the text from the 14th century onwards.
It lost ground in the 16th century as humanists preferred Greek and Roman authorities to Arabic ones, but it was still taught as background literature in Padua in 1715.
dyk: The Canon gives seven rules for experimenting with new drugs, taken partly from Galen, among them that a drug should be tested on a single condition rather than a composite one and that experiments should be carried out on the human body.

sections.origins:
The medical traditions of Galen, and through him Hippocrates, had dominated Islamic medicine from its beginnings. The Canon presents an overview of the medical knowledge of the Islamic world, which had also been influenced by Persian, Chinese and Indian medicine. Galen's own medical writings ran to twenty volumes, and a more concise reference was wanted in contrast to them.

Its author, Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, sought to fit these inherited traditions into Aristotle's natural philosophy. The result is described as a clear and ordered summa of all the medical knowledge of his time. The title in Arabic is al-Qanun fi l-tibb. The word qanun, often translated as law or legal code, here suggests an ordered system or a complete, universal encyclopedia. The common medieval Latin title was Canon Medicinae or Liber Canonis, from which the English title comes.

Ibn Sina defined medicine (tibb) as the science by which we learn the various states of the body, in health and when not in health, the means by which health is likely to be lost and, when lost, is likely to be restored. He held that the body cannot be restored to health unless the causes of both health and disease are determined.
sections.content:
The Canon is divided into five books. Book 1 gives essays on basic medical and physiological principles, anatomy, regimen and general therapeutic procedures. Book 2 lists medical substances alphabetically after an essay on their general properties. Book 3 treats the diagnosis and treatment of diseases specific to one part of the body, and Book 4 conditions that cover several parts or the whole body. Book 5 is a formulary of compound remedies. Books 1, 3 and 4 are further divided into parts, chapters, subchapters, sections and subsections.

Book 1 holds six theses on the cosmic elements, the temperaments, the humours, anatomy and physiology, and explains the causes of health and disease. Book 2 lists about 800 simple floral, mineral and animal substances, each with its criteria of goodness, its nature, one or more of 22 possible general actions and its substitutes. Book 3 runs from head to foot through the organs and their diseases. Book 4 gives long sections to fevers, divided into ephemeral, putrid and hectic kinds, and ends with a treatise on personal hygiene. Book 5 lists 650 compound drugs, attributed to Arabic, Indian and Greek sources.
sections.making:
Ibn Sina began writing the Canon in Gorganj, continued in Rey and completed it in Hamadan in 1025. He built it on the Four Humours of Hippocratic medicine but refined them. In explaining how disease arises he added his own view of different types of spirits, or vital life essences, and souls, whose disturbances might lead to bodily diseases through their close association with master organs such as the brain and heart.

In his account of the body he set out four causes of illness taken from Aristotelian philosophy: material, efficient, formal and final. He took the Aristotelian view that the heart is the ultimate source of the body's faculties, against Galen's view that the brain is the chief seat of sentient life, while allowing that the brain is where the rational faculty shows itself. In Book 5 he commented on differences between recipes from different sources, sometimes gave his own, and favoured remedies proven by experience, cautioning that compounds could have unexpected or much stronger effects than their separate components.

The thesis on the elements, which Oskar Cameron Gruner calls the foundation of the whole Canon, insists that a physician must assume the four elements of natural philosophy. In another work, the Treatise on Pulse, Ibn Sina combined his own view of spirits with that of the Four Humours to form a new doctrine of how various diseases arise.
sections.reception:
The Canon remained a medical authority for centuries and set the standards for medicine in medieval Europe and the Islamic world. Its encyclopaedic content, systematic arrangement and combination of Galen's medicine with Aristotle's science and philosophy helped it enter European scholastic medicine. Medical scholars started to use it in the 13th century, and university courses implemented the text from the 14th century onwards.

Its influence declined in the 16th century because humanists preferred ancient Greek and Roman authorities in medicine to Arabic ones, although others defended Avicenna's innovations beyond the original classical texts. It fell out of favour in university syllabi but was still being taught as background literature as late as 1715 in Padua. It is also an important text in Unani medicine, a form of traditional medicine practised in India. William Osler described it as the most famous medical textbook ever written and said it remained a medical bible for a longer time than any other work. George Sarton, in his Introduction to the History of Science, called it an immense encyclopedia of medicine.
sections.survival:
The earliest known copy of volume 5, dated 1052, is held in the collection of the Aga Khan and housed in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto. The earliest printed edition of the Latin Canon appeared in 1472 and covered only book three. Soon afterwards eleven complete incunables were published, followed by fourteen more Latin editions in the 16th century, the last in 1608.

The Canon was translated from Arabic into Latin as Canon medicinae by a Gerard of Cremona; there appear to have been two men of that name, both translators of Arabic texts into Latin. Besides Latin, it was translated into Hebrew by Nathan ha-Meati during the 13th century, and complete translations were made into Turkish and Persian during the 18th century. Gruner's English edition of the first book, a treatise on the Canon with a translation of Book 1, was published in 1973, and an English version of volume 1 appeared in 1999.

Its place in European teaching ended gradually. It fell out of favour in university syllabi in the 16th century, though it was still being taught as background literature as late as 1715 in Padua. In the Islamic world and India it remained an important text in Unani medicine.
sections.legacy:
The Canon was used as a standard medical textbook through the 18th century in Europe, and its Latin translation greatly influenced the development of medieval medicine. Its rules for testing new drugs, its description of strokes, its long chapter on the nervous system and its treatment of fevers have all been studied by later readers.

Modern authors have examined particular passages. The information in Book 3 is described as representing some of Avicenna's most important contributions to several fields, including atherosclerosis, pulsology, migraines, cataracts, vasovagal syncope and neuroscience. In its account of stroke, based on humoral medicine, the descriptions are still similar to the modern understanding of the condition. Book 3 lists fifteen kinds of headache and names conditions from epilepsy and paralysis to melancholia and insomnia, with treatments in three steps: a change of lifestyle, simple medicines and compound medicines, with surgery or other non-drug methods in some cases. Sarton singled out its thoughts on the contagious nature of phthisis and its descriptions of skin and nervous ailments.

summary: The Canon of Medicine is Ibn Sina's five-book encyclopedia of medicine, completed in Hamadan in 1025. Translated into Latin, it entered European scholastic medicine and served as a standard textbook in universities into the early modern period.
